narrative:
The model estimates an 88% probability that you will leave your job, and that high predicted flight risk is why you are being denied a promotion at this time. This is a probability, not a certainty, but it is strong enough that the organization is treating retention risk as the deciding factor.

The most influential signal was your total years of work experience. At 6–10 years, you have more accumulated experience than the typical employee predicted to stay, most of whom have only 1–5 years. This pushed the prediction toward leaving. The second-strongest signal was that you already have other job opportunities; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay reported the same, so this strongly increased the leaving prediction. The third signal was your tenure with your current organization. Being in the 1–5 year range is common among stayers, but in your overall profile it still added to the leaving risk rather than reducing it.

These factors outweighed your recognition, useful training, and general job satisfaction. Next, the organization should discuss your career path, promotion criteria, and retention options openly, especially given your experience and external opportunities. You should ask for clear feedback on what would change the decision, and consider whether your development and rewards here match your goals.
